catalog_quote: Tyhurst (1984) and Mbuagbaw (1994) identified four basic tones in Kenyang: two level tones, high [ ´] and low [ `], and two contour tones, rising [ ˇ] and falling [ ˆ]. Tone wa represented lexically within morphemes and grammatically within sentences. ... 4.1 Tonal Contrast. Tones in Kenyang contrast minimally. The speaker uses the pitch of his voice to distinguish lexically between morphemes and words which would have been otherwise identical. For example, tone minimally distinguishes the following words: (1) [èβá] fence / [èβà] bag / [m̀mú] dog / [m̀mù] person / [fǎ] give way / [fâ] here / [ŋ̀kɔ́k] ladder / ŋ̀kɔ̀k] fowl

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kenyang is described as a tone language with two level tones (H, L) and two contour tones (rising, falling), plus downstepped H mentioned later (p. 10-11); tone is contrastive lexically (e.g. [èβá] 'fence' vs [èβà] 'bag', [m̀mú] 'dog' vs [m̀mù] 'person') and grammatically (tense/aspect). The source makes no statement whatsoever about word stress or accent placement; no stress rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; tone orthography issues (downstep vs high, falling vs low) discussed pp. 10-11.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on morphemes/words (citation forms in minimal pairs) and grammatical tone within sentences; nothing on phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: The 1998 lexicon and the SIL materials describe standard (Upper) Kenyang of Manyu Division, Cameroon, as written by the Society for Kenyang Literature; no dialect is specified. Ittmann 1935-36 'Sprache der Nyang' and Glottolog/WALS treat this as the same language (keny1279 / ISO ken; WALS kyg).

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing statement (Mbuagbaw 1998 lexicon: tone language with four tones H, L, rising, falling; no stress statement); adds downstep as an orthographic category. Silent on stress itself. Names Lower Kenyang as the standard reference dialect (p. 4) and lists the three dialects Upper Kenyang, Lower Kenyang, Kitwii (p. 1).
new_statements.rule_in_words: A language-development case study, not a phonology. It confirms that Kenyang is a tone language whose orthography marks high, rising, falling and downstepped tones (low unmarked; from 1998 only high and rising marked). It says nothing about word stress, accent or prominence (a full-text search for stress/accent|accent|prominen|suprasegment: 0 hits in the 7 pages).
new_statements.exceptions: none (the only tone remarks concern which tones the orthography marks; the diacritic glyphs are missing from the text and were read from the rendered page scan)
new_statements.identity_note: Both Mbuagbaw works describe Kenyang (ISO ken) as spoken in Manyu and Meme Divisions, South West Province, Cameroon; Mbuagbaw 2008 (pp. 1, 4) names three dialects, Upper Kenyang, Lower Kenyang and Kitwii, and records that Lower Kenyang was chosen as the standard reference dialect, which agrees with the 1998 Lexicon's statement that its entries come from Lower Kenyang. Mbuagbaw 2000 (p. 9) notes Koelle's 1854 wordlist came from a speaker of the Lower Kenyang dialect area. The tone statements are for the language as a whole (reference dialect Lower Kenyang). Tyhurst 1985 is on Kenyang tone (noun phrases); its dialect is unknown.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing statement (tone language, four tones: H, L, rising LH, falling HL; no stress statement). Silent on stress itself, so it neither confirms nor refutes any stress placement; it adds that the syllable (including syllabic nasals) is the tone-bearing unit and that semi-vowels are toneless.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A segmental phonology (vowels, consonants, syllable structure, processes). It treats the syllable as the tone-bearing unit and lists the tones H, L, LH, HL, but explicitly defers tone to a separate 'Kenyang tone system' and never mentions stress, accent or prominence anywhere in the 92 pages (a full-text search for stress/accent|accent|prominen|suprasegment|intensity: 0 hits; the only prosodic remark is that semi-vowels do not carry a contrastive tone of their own, p. 48). The literature review (p. 10) cites Tyhurst's 1984 preliminary phonology and 1986 MA thesis 'Tone System of Kenyang Noun Phrase' and Odden 1988 on floating and contour tones.
new_statements.identity_note: Both Mbuagbaw works describe Kenyang (ISO ken) as spoken in Manyu and Meme Divisions, South West Province, Cameroon; Mbuagbaw 2008 (pp. 1, 4) names three dialects, Upper Kenyang, Lower Kenyang and Kitwii, and records that Lower Kenyang was chosen as the standard reference dialect, which agrees with the 1998 Lexicon's statement that its entries come from Lower Kenyang. Mbuagbaw 2000 (p. 9) notes Koelle's 1854 wordlist came from a speaker of the Lower Kenyang dialect area. The tone statements are for the language as a whole (reference dialect Lower Kenyang). Tyhurst 1985 is on Kenyang tone (noun phrases); its dialect is unknown.

new_statements.quote: [p. 9, section 3 'Lexical Tone'] There are two phonological tones, High (H) and Low (L). It is possible for two different tonemes to be linked to a single vowel and this results in a phonetic contour tone. Both of the logical possibilities, Falling (HL) and Rising (LH), are realized in surface forms. [...] [p. 12, 3.2.1] The set of tone bearing units consists of syllable peaks, i.e. vowels and syllabic nasals. [...] [p. 14, on an OCP-based alternative] We must either (a) assume that tones are lexically associated; or (b) adopt a system of accents. Both solutions are unappealing, because they fail to express the restrictions on tone distributions in a systematic way.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's 'tonal' coding (Mbuagbaw 1998, which itself cites 'Tyhurst (1984)' for the four basic tones H, L, rising, falling) and with the three statements held by the project (all 'tone language, no stress statement'). Adds primary-source detail: the underlying inventory is two level tones (H, L) with rising/falling as HL/LH sequences on one vowel rather than four basic tones; TBUs = vowels and syllabic nasals; three-tone root melodies; downstep and non-iterative downdrift with 'upstep' of the last H before a linked L. Like the works held by the project it says nothing about word stress, so the catalog reading (tonal, no stress statement) stands; no contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kenyang (Lower Kenyang dialect) is analysed as a tone language with two phonological tones, H and L; falling and rising contours are two tonemes on one vowel; tone-bearing units are vowels and syllabic nasals; noun roots carry three-tone melodies associated left-to-right; downstep (from floating L, 'LH Simplification') and downdrift are described (section 6). Nothing anywhere in the thesis (all 62 pages examined: 40 by scanned, 22 as page scan) mentions word stress, syllable prominence or intensity; the only use of 'accent' (pp. 14-15) is a Goldsmith-style diacritic-accent device for tone association, which the author considers and rejects ('Both solutions are unappealing'; 'I conclude that the OCP is not a valid principle in the Kenyang lexicon'). No statement that stress exists, where it would fall, or that it is absent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned (no stress discussed at all)
new_statements.exceptions: n/a for stress. Tonal details: nasal prefixes never bear H (pp. 7, 16-18, unexplained in the analysis); contour tones only on monosyllabic noun roots, never on prefixes or bisyllabic roots (p. 9; one apparent counter-example note 3, p. 49); the associative-marker deletion rule differs between the Egbekaw and Bachuo Ntai sub-dialects (pp. 25-27).
new_statements.identity_note: Lower Kenyang dialect spoken near Mamfe, Manyu Division, Southwest Province, Cameroon; data from the villages of Egbekaw (principal source) and Bachuo Ntai (p. 1, p. iv, p. 25-27). The thesis names three mutually intelligible dialects: Lower Kenyang, Upper Kenyang, Kitwii (pp. 1-2). Same language as keny1279 / ISO ken; the catalog's reference dialect (Mbuagbaw: Lower Kenyang) is the same variety.

General conclusion (p. 111): the Nyang languages have two underlying tones H and L; tone reconstruction for Proto-Nyang was NOT attempted and is left for future work.
